claim: A web app builds its property definitions from a shape the workstation page service answers, so a change to what a shape carries reaches no browser until the workstation services are put up, however many times the web app itself is deployed.

evidence:
`filePropertyDefinitions` builds every definition from `shapeAsked`, which calls `shapeFor(pageTypeSlug)`, and `shapeFor` is a call over HTTP to the page service. `definitionOf` can only carry what the shape holds, so a field `declaredOf` learns to read is absent from the browser's definitions while the service answering shapes runs older code.

The page service runs on the workstation, out of `.git/trees/service-workstation`, and that tree moves when the workstation services are put up rather than when a commit lands. `akasha deploy` refuses a single workstation service by name and says to name `service-workstation`, which reaches every workstation unit at once.

Measured 2026-09-21 on `feature-request`. Commit `5680c8e7372` landed `verbId` on `Declared` at 16:01 MDT. The requests pod was rebuilt at `c7709e1a0f7` and `/api/pages/page-type` answered the `back` property as `{"type": "action-button", "config": {}}`, so the browser drew the button disabled. A POST of `{"pageTypeSlug":"feature-request"}` to the page service answered a `back` declaration carrying no `verbId` key at all, while `targetSlug` and `values` were both there as null. `.git/trees/service-workstation` sat at `3897e70e7c6`, landed 15:43 MDT, eighteen minutes before the change.
